title: Germany and France Just Scrapped the Transit Visa for Indians. Here's Why It Matters.
excerpt: Indian passport holders can now connect through Frankfurt, Munich, and Paris without extra paperwork — a quiet win that opens up competitive long-haul routing across Europe.
body:
For decades, Indian passport holders booking a connecting flight through Frankfurt or Munich had to navigate an absurdity: a separate visa application, a €60 fee, five to seven days of processing time, and the ever-present risk of being offloaded at the gate — all just to sit in an airport transit lounge they were never going to leave.

That requirement is now gone. Germany officially scrapped the airport transit visa for Indian nationals on June 3, 2026, following France's identical move. The two countries that operate Europe's busiest aviation hubs have effectively dismantled the last major barrier between Indian travelers and competitive long-haul routing through the continent.

## What Changed

The German Embassy in New Delhi confirmed that the exemption was published in the Federal Law Gazette (Bundesgesetzblatt) on June 2 and took immediate effect. The policy change implements a commitment made during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to India in January 2026, which also produced new agreements on skilled worker mobility and technology cooperation.

Under the new rules, Indian passport holders can transit through any German airport's international zone without a Schengen Type A visa, provided they hold a confirmed onward ticket and do not cross border control into the country.

France had already waived the requirement at Charles de Gaulle and other airports, matching a policy that countries like the Netherlands (via Amsterdam-Schiphol) had adopted years earlier.

## Why This Matters for NRIs and Indian Travelers

The practical impact is enormous. Germany's Frankfurt Airport is the third-busiest hub in Europe and a critical node for Lufthansa's global network. Millions of Indians — students, business travelers, Gulf workers, and tourists — route through German airports annually on their way to North America, the UK, Africa, and Latin America.

Previously, booking a competitive connecting fare through Frankfurt meant first navigating a separate visa process at the German consulate. Travel managers estimated the full cost — application fees, courier charges, and lost productivity — at ₹5,500 to ₹7,000 per trip. For frequent travelers, the cumulative burden was enough to avoid German hubs entirely, even when they offered the cheapest fares.

Airlines are expected to benefit significantly. Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners can now market Indian connections more aggressively, and Air India stands to expand its code-share arrangements through German airports. Industry forecasts project a 10-12% jump in India-Germany transit traffic by year's end.

This change is particularly significant for the Indian diaspora in the US, UK, and Canada, who often travel to India via European hubs. The removal of the transit visa requirement not only simplifies travel logistics but also enhances the ability of NRIs to maintain family ties and manage business commitments back home, ultimately supporting remittances and economic connections.

## A Broader Pattern

The transit visa removal fits into a larger diplomatic narrative. India and Germany have steadily deepened their strategic partnership under what both sides describe as a "Year of Innovation 2026" framework. Merz's January visit — his first bilateral trip after taking office — signaled that Berlin views India as a priority market and a counterweight to China in technology supply chains.

France's parallel move reflects similar thinking. President Emmanuel Macron has invited Prime Minister Narendra Modi to the G7 summit in Évian later this month, where AI governance, energy security, and Global South representation are expected to dominate the agenda. Modi will also attend VivaTech in Paris on June 18, Europe's largest technology startup event, and is expected to address the Indian diaspora in France.

For the estimated 10 million Indians who hold valid passports and travel internationally at least once a year — a number that has doubled since 2019 — these changes represent a concrete improvement in the travel experience. No more consulate appointments for a 90-minute layover. No more routing through more expensive alternatives to avoid German airspace.

## What Stays the Same

The exemption applies strictly to airport transit. Indians planning to enter Germany — for tourism, business, or study — still need a standard Schengen visa. The transit exemption also does not cover overland border crossings or rail connections, only international airport zones.

For NRIs in the United States, Canada, and the UK who frequently fly to India through European hubs, the change opens up routing options that were previously off the table or required extra paperwork. Combined with competitive Lufthansa fares to Indian metros, the Frankfurt and Munich corridors are likely to see a sharp increase in Indian passenger traffic.

The last major European transit visa barrier for Indian travelers has now been removed. The Indian passport, long ranked among the least powerful in the world for visa-free travel, just gained two of Europe's most important airports as frictionless waypoints. As Indian travelers share their experiences and the travel industry adapts, this policy change is set to reshape the landscape of international travel for the Indian diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
